newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIAN BANKS-Lending priorities handicap banks.
newsitem.headline: INDIAN BANKS-Lending priorities handicap banks.

text.p: "Priority sector" lending locks up a large chunk of Indian bank funds in low-yielding assets and there is little hope of change in the debilitating system in the near future, analysts and bankers said on Thursday.
"The government is basically committed to helping the weaker sections of society and banks have a role to play in this," said K.R. Ramamoorthy, chief executive of private sector Vysya Bank.
"In the immediate future, there is little likelihood of priority sector targets being reduced."
Currently all Indian banks are required to lend a minimum of 40 percent of their net credit (loans less repayments) to areas designated as priority sectors.

These include agriculture and allied activities, small businesses, small-scale industry and "socially and economically backward classes" -- an euphemism for the poorest among India's population of 940 million.
Foreign banks have a lower priority sector lending target of 32 percent because their branch network is limited and branch expansion is subject to central bank licencing policies.

Banks that fail to achieve priority sector targets have to deposit an amount equivalent to the shortfall with specialised institutions such as the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund or the Small Scale Industrial Development Bank of India.
Banks earn between 8.0 and 12.5 percent on these deposits, thus losing out on opportunity cost as the lowest prime lending rate is 13.5 percent.
Inevitably, the rules have hit banks' bottom lines.
An expert group on financial reforms suggested in 1991 that priority sector lending should be slashed to 10 percent of net bank credit from 40 percent.
The rates of interest on priority sector loans are fixed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and banks are free to determine interest only for loans above 200,000 rupees ($5,600).
Loans for amounts below 200,000 rupees are fixed by the RBI and are below bank prime lending rates to commercial borrowers.
"Priority sector lending rates are by and large below prime (lending rates)," said Sandeep Nanda, banking analyst at NatWest Markets. "This hits bank revenue streams."
"But I think a bigger problem is the incidence of bad loans in the priority sector," he said.
Bankers admit that small loans are inadequately monitored and recovery rates poor, leading to a high level of bad loans.
They said this was one reason why banks failed to achieve targets for lending to the priority sector.
For the year ended March 31, 1996, public sector banks as a group had reached a level of 37.8 percent and private banks 32.5 percent against the required 40 percent.
Foreign banks, unlike Indian banks are allowed to include export credit as priority sector lending and this has helped them attain a level of 39 percent.
"One big loan of five million rupees requires say a couple of officers for monitoring," said the chairman of a Bombay-based state-run bank.
"If I have to lend the same in priority, I end up having to lend to 20,000 people. It means that many more accounts to monitor and that much more effort and manpower locked up."
Other industry observers differ and say banks are looking for an easy way out to avoid social obligations.
"I think it is more of an attitude problem on the part of bankers," said Bandi Ramprasad, chief economist of the Indian Banks' Association.
"The major strength of Indian banks, particularly state-run banks is their network in rural and semi-urban areas. It should not be difficult to lend to the priority sector," he said.
Ramprasad said interest rates had come down in the current year on the back of good liquidity and the differential between priority sector loans and commercial loans had narrowed.
Bankers said one way to overcome banks' reluctance to lend to such sectors could be by redefining priority sectors.
"We as a bank have no problem with the concept of priority sector lending," said Paresh Sukthankar, head of credit and market risk at private-sector HDFC Bank.
"Why shouldn't lending to power, roads, telcommunications be not classified as priority sector? Why should they be any less priority than agriculture?" he asked. ($1 = 35.7 rupees)
